claims.text: Simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature accelerates degradation in multi-phase eutectic HEAs.
The accelerated coupled degradation is driven by cyclic rupture of protective oxide films at interphase boundaries.
Film rupture exposes heterogeneous phase interfaces that establish local galvanic cells.
The local galvanic cells synergistically accelerate both wear and corrosion.
The relevant initial material is an as-cast, finely segregated eutectic HEA.
The eutectic microstructure can comprise an FCC matrix and dispersed sigma phase.
Intact passivating oxide films are located along the interphase boundaries in the initial material.
Testing at approximately 350 degrees Celsius ensures dynamic oxide-film formation and rupture.
Mechanical friction or wear disrupts a surface oxide film and contributes to adhesive and abrasive wear.
Compositional and electrochemical differences between FCC and sigma phases promote localized galvanic corrosion.
Galvanic differences between phases can cause selective anodic dissolution in eutectic HEAs.
Repeated film rupture and corrosion weaken the material and thereby increase subsequent wear.
Total degradation under combined wear and corrosion will significantly exceed the arithmetic sum of isolated wear and corrosion losses.
Wear-volume loss under combined wear and corrosion will be markedly higher than in the wear-only test.
Corrosion-current density under combined wear and corrosion will be markedly higher than in the corrosion-only test.
Increasing temperature can increase selective dissolution in a eutectic HEA.
The proposed mechanism applies near 350 degrees Celsius when dynamic oxide-film formation and rupture occur.
Real-time surface microscopy and EIS can identify cyclic oxide-film rupture specifically at interphase boundaries.
An additive-or-lower combined degradation response, or absence of cyclic interphase film rupture, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions call for constant electrolyte composition and the falsification design describes identical environmental conditions, but the wear-only control uses an inert electrolyte while the combined and corrosion-only tests use the corrosive electrolyte. These controls are therefore not environmentally identical.
The baseline is described as using the same temperature and electrolyte settings, yet its wear-only arm changes to an inert electrolyte to suppress corrosion.
